title: A Practical Trophy Archive for a Community Club
description: Plan a manageable community club trophy archive, organise source photographs, review winner records and hand the collection over to the next committee.
html:
Community club history often survives in several places at once: a trophy cabinet, an honours book, committee minutes and the memories of long-standing members. An archive project begins by bringing those sources into an organised process. It does not need to begin with the entire cabinet.

Agree what the first stage will cover

Choose a competition, a group of trophies or a defined period. Record the scope in a note the committee can understand. “Review the winners engraved on the Captain’s Cup from its first visible year to the latest entry” gives volunteers a clearer starting point than “digitise our history.”

List the trophies in that first stage, where each is kept and who has permission to handle it. Include any alternative competition names so a later reviewer can recognise the same award in an old result sheet.

Gather the sources before resolving the story

Take a photograph of each complete trophy, followed by close views of the engraved areas. For lettering around a base, use overlapping photographs. Note where supporting records can be found and retain the originals. A transcript is a working interpretation of the source, not a substitute for it.

Ask long-standing members where records may be held. Their knowledge can guide research, but distinguish a recollection from a documented result. If you use a minute book to resolve a name, record the relevant date or page in the club’s project notes.

Agree simple review conventions

  • Keep the engraved initials unless reliable evidence supports expanding them.
  • Check that every entered year belongs to the correct competition.
  • Distinguish the text on the trophy from a later correction supported by another source.
  • Leave an unresolved gap visible in the working process.
  • Ask a second person to check difficult or important interpretations where possible.

A well-documented incomplete archive can be improved when new evidence appears. An apparently complete list containing guesses is harder for the next committee to trust.

Separate a working archive from a public board

The reviewers need source photographs and room to correct records. Members browsing the club’s history need a clear presentation of the information the club has approved for sharing. Decide who can authorise publication and which records are ready.

In Trophy Guru, the private working archive supports reviewing trophy photographs and winner records. A published honours board is a separate presentation, with views by year, trophy and person. Publication does not give visitors access to private source photographs or member matching information. Read the archive and publication controls before sharing.

Plan the handover from the beginning

Record who coordinates the archive and how the next volunteer will receive responsibility. Keep an exported copy of reviewed records in a location the club controls. Agree when the latest competition results will be added and who will check them. An archive that can survive a committee change is more useful than one dependent on a single person’s memory.

Do not treat CSV export as a complete copy of every uploaded photograph or every application setting. Check what the export contains, retain your original sources separately and open the exported file to confirm that it is usable.

Start with one trophy your club knows

The committee project plan provides a pilot and handover checklist. The practical cataloguing guide covers capture and review, while our public demo shows how members can explore the result. Trophy Guru’s first trophy is free, with up to 12 saved photographs and no card required. Start there and use what you learn to plan the next batch.
